cases.question: What are the design principles of the Sustainability pillar?

cases.answer:
The design principles for sustainability in the cloud are:

• Design for flexibility to allow for the rapid adoption of new efficient technologies. [1][2][3]
• Align computational approach to problem complexity: Apply the least resource-intensive approach that satisfies the business requirement. [1][2][3]
• Minimize the footprint of data and its processing: Retain only data with a defined business purpose, assigning every data set a business owner and an expiration date. [2]
• Maximize utilization: Right-size workloads and implement efficient design to drive high utilization and maximize the energy efficiency of the underlying hardware. [3]
• Anticipate and adopt new, more efficient hardware and software offerings: Support the upstream improvements your partners and suppliers make to help you reduce the impact of your cloud workloads. [3]
• Understand your impact: Measure the impact of your cloud workload and model the future impact of your workload. [4]
• Establish sustainability goals: For each cloud workload, establish long-term sustainability goals such as reducing the compute and storage resources required per transaction. [4]

cases.question: How should I design for failure?
retrieved: 0.723 Cloud Workloads > Reliability > Design your workload to withstand component failures p.765

0.701 Cloud Workloads > Reliability > Design interactions in a distributed system to mitigate or withstand failures p.653
cases.answer:
To design for failure, you should:

* Design each workload to expect failures and keep serving customers when they happen [1]
* Detect faults at every layer [REL11-BP01]
* Fail over to healthy resources [REL11-BP02]
* Automate healing on all layers [REL11-BP03]
* Rely on the data plane and not the control plane during recovery [REL11-BP04]
* Use static stability to prevent bimodal behavior [REL11-BP05]
* Send notifications when events impact availability [REL11-BP06]
* Design your workload to withstand component failures, detecting faults at every layer, failing over to healthy resources, automating recovery, keeping recovery actions on the most available paths, holding capacity in advance for static stability, notifying teams even when automation resolves an event, and designing to the availability target the business set [1]

Additionally, consider implementing:

* Graceful degradation to transform hard dependencies into soft dependencies [REL05-BP01]
* Fault isolation to contain the scope of a failure [section "Failure management" [3]]
* Backing up data [section "Failure management" [3]]
* Using the circuit breaker pattern to stop calls after failures cross a threshold and periodically probe for recovery [section "Design interactions in a distributed system to mitigate or withstand failures" [4]]
* Using the saga pattern to roll back completed operations if a later one fails, preserving consistency [section "Design interactions in a distributed system to mitigate or withstand failures" [4]]

To protect data at rest, you should combine encryption with access controls. [2] Encryption renders data unreadable without the key, while access controls decide who can reach it. [2] Additionally, consider using tokenization, data masking, and other techniques to match the sensitivity of the data and the obligations that apply to it. [2]

It is also recommended to enforce encryption at rest by making it the default for new resources and keeping an inventory of any unencrypted data. [4] Furthermore, automation can help enforce controls continuously, catch misconfigurations before deployment, and remediate drift at runtime. [1] This includes using infrastructure as code (IaC) to inspect and reject noncompliant changes before deployment, and runtime monitoring tools to detect changes to encryption and other controls. [3]

0.813 Cloud Foundations > Resource and inventory management > FND04-BP05 Establish service quota management p.144
cases.answer:
To manage service quotas, follow these steps:

* Designate a delegated administrator for Service Quotas, typically your central operations or foundation account, to manage quotas across the organization without holding member-account credentials [2].
* Inventory current quota consumption using the Quota Monitor for AWS solution to identify quotas close to their limits, quotas that are likely undersized for current workload trajectories, and quotas that are irrelevant to your workloads [2].
* Establish a baseline quota profile per account type, using different baselines for sandbox, development, and production, and apply the production baseline automatically when an account is marked as production [4].
* Use Service Quotas templates to manage quotas, including quota request templates to new accounts automatically, including accounts vended through AWS Control Tower Account Factory [4].
* Set thresholds well below 100%, such as 70-80%, to alert when consumption approaches configured thresholds, giving workload and foundation teams time to request increases before workloads hit the limit [4].
* Review and adjust quotas regularly to ensure they are aligned with workload growth and scaling needs.
